To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Hsp70-peptides can be applied to enhance cytolytic activity and tumor recognition of NK cells in vivo.
the reinfusion of autologous NK lymphocytes that had been stimulated ex vivo by Hsp70-peptides is safe and may enhance the cytolytic potential of NK cells against tumors.
the Hsp70 peptide TKD activates NK cells, and that reinfusion of these cells into cancer patients is safe.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of immunotherapeutic concepts for cancer patients based on the use of autologous NK and T cells.
the identification of tumor-selective structures on the cell membrane of cancer cells.
the identification and characterization of novel, tumor-specific recognition structures on the cell surface.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this is the first clinical trial with Hsp70-primed NK cells in cancer patients and the results are promising.
this is a pilot Phase I study, which has shown the feasibility of this approach and has provided some evidence of clinical benefit.
this study was a proof of concept that the Hsp70-activating NK cell approach was feasible in a clinical setting and was safe for the patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Hsp70-activating NK cells are a promising tool to treat metastasized cancer patients.
the Hsp70-activation of NK cells is an effective way of enhancing the NK-cell cytotoxicity in vitro and in patients.
we are able to activate the NK cells in vitro and to reinfuse them into the patient.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Hsp70-activation of NK cells is safe and can induce a tumor cell–specific immune response.
Hsp70 is an excellent tumor-associated target antigen for NK cells.
we can now activate NK cells in a safe way, and this is an important step in our quest to use NK cells in cancer therapy.
